Can you provide answers for the sections below? We try to collect concise, operational answers to feed into our vendor review:

1) Which uptime window and metric do you use for the platform-wide availability SLO (e.g., service request availability, control plane vs data plane)?
2) How are latency SLOs defined (percentile, route-level vs global)? Any per-model considerations?
3) What monitoring tooling do you ingest for your own SLOs and what we can expect to see if granted access?
4) Alerting thresholds and on-call rotation for production incidents that impact SLOs.
5) If you need an exception (for example, short maintenance that impacts a subset of regions), what is the approval path and typical turnaround?
6) What level of dashboard access can a customer get (read-only dashboards, raw metrics export, alert subscriptions)?

If you can get this back by end of day Tuesday (20th) that would be great — procurement will use it for the next-step security/finance review.

Hi James —

Appreciate the clear list. Attached is a short PDF with operational answers and links to the dashboards we can grant. High-level answers inline below; see the PDF for specifics and example queries.

1) Availability: We measure availability on the data plane (token generation endpoints) as a per-region request success rate over a 30-day rolling window. The SLO is 99.95% for production Dedicated customers; hosted tiers have a 99.9% published target. Control plane (model catalog, billing API) is measured separately and not included in the data-plane SLO.

2) Latency: Latency SLOs are defined per-route and per-model by percentile (p50/p95/p99) with p95 as the contractual target for interactive workloads. For larger batch/embeddings endpoints we publish a throughput-targeted latency band. We include model-specific profiles in the attachment for typical p95 numbers on the common model families.

3) Monitoring tooling: We use an internal metrics pipeline that exports to Prometheus-compatible backends and Grafana for dashboards. For procurement customers we can grant a read-only Grafana view and a limited scrape of metric series via a CSV export. We also include synthetic checks (regional heartbeats) aggregated into the availability metric.

4) Alerting/on-call: Alert thresholds are derived from SLO burn rates (standard SRE practice). On-call follows a two-tier rotation: platform on-call (24/7) and inference runtime escalation (engineers). Major incidents that threaten the SLO trigger a pager; non-severity incidents use Slack + ticketing. Typical initial response SLA is 15 minutes for pages.

5) Exceptions: We maintain an exception registry. Short maintenance events that impact <5% of traffic in a region can be approved by the operations lead (1–2 business days). Exceptions that would cause a persistent SLO deviation or cross-region impact require product/CS sign-off and are reviewed within 3–5 business days. We document approved exceptions in the customer’s procurement packet.

6) Customer access: Customers get read-only Grafana dashboards, a delivery of the last 30 days of raw time series (CSV), and the ability to subscribe to SLO burn rate alerts. For Dedicated customers we can extend a private dashboard instance with per-route filters.

I attached the PDF with measurement queries and a CSV template for the dashboard invite. Happy to set up a short call to walk through the dashboards.

—
Vanessa Ortiz
Senior Solutions Engineer, Redwood Inference

James — quick technical clarifications from the infra side (copied Vanessa):

- The availability SLO (data plane) excludes customer-side network failures and client-side timeouts; we use a service-side status code + success window to evaluate.
- For p95 measurement we use ingest-point latency (time from request acceptance to token-stream completion) and compute percentiles on trimmed windows to avoid outliers from background garbage collection events.
- For multi-model routing, we tag metrics by model-family and route; customers on Dedicated can opt into unsampled traces for debug with restricted access.

If Acme expects a shorter exception approval window for scheduled maintenance (e.g., a coordinated migration), we can pre-authorize a maintenance ticket with product and reduce approval to <24 hours. Otherwise the standard 1–2 business day path applies.

-Karthik
Principal Reliability Engineer, Redwood Inference
